interactions.label: The narration states that gut movements continue even under general anaesthesia.

params.question: The narration states that gut movements continue even under general anaesthesia. Which of the following best explains this observation?

answers.text: Sympathetic nerves from the spinal cord maintain gut motility during anaesthesia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sympathetic stimulation actually inhibits gut motility. It is the fight-or-flight division, which diverts resources away from digestion.

answers.text: The enteric nervous system, with approximately 500 million neurons, operates as an independent neural network within the gut wall

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The ENS contains about 500 million neurons in Meissner's and Auerbach's plexuses and can generate coordinated gut movements independently of the central nervous system.

answers.text: Circulating gut hormones such as motilin sustain peristalsis regardless of the depth of anaesthesia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While motilin drives the migrating myoelectric complex during fasting, ongoing peristalsis under anaesthesia is due to the intrinsic enteric nervous system, not circulating hormones.

answers.text: Skeletal muscle in the oesophagus maintains the propulsive force throughout the alimentary canal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Skeletal muscle is limited to the pharynx and upper oesophagus. The rest of the alimentary canal uses smooth muscle coordinated by the enteric nervous system.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the concept of the enteric nervous system. It contains ~500 million neurons in two plexuses (Meissner's and Auerbach's) and can function independently of the brain and spinal cord.
Well done. The enteric nervous system is rightly called the 'second brain' — its independent function is why gut motility persists even when the CNS is suppressed.

interactions.label: Salivary secretion is regulated by both neural and hormonal mechanisms, similar

params.question: Salivary secretion is regulated by both neural and hormonal mechanisms, similar to gastric and pancreatic secretions.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is actually false. Salivation is unique among GI secretions — it is controlled entirely by the nervous system (parasympathetic and sympathetic), with no hormonal input. Gastric and pancreatic secretions, by contrast, are regulated by both neural and hormonal mechanisms.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Unlike gastric and pancreatic secretions, salivation is controlled entirely by neural reflexes: parasympathetic stimulation produces copious watery saliva, while sympathetic stimulation produces thick mucous secretion. No GI hormone regulates salivary output.

interactions.label: Why are pancreatic proteolytic enzymes secreted as inactive zymogens rather than

params.question: Why are pancreatic proteolytic enzymes secreted as inactive zymogens rather than in their active form?

answers.text: Active enzymes would be destroyed by acidic gastric juice before reaching the duodenum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pancreatic enzymes enter the duodenum directly through the pancreatic duct, not through the stomach. The zymogen strategy protects the pancreas itself, not the enzymes from acid.

answers.text: Zymogens are more concentrated and potent than active enzymes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Zymogens are inactive precursors that must be cleaved to become functional. They have no enzymatic activity until activated — they are not more potent.

answers.text: Inactive zymogens prevent the pancreas from digesting its own tissue

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Zymogens remain inactive until enterokinase in the duodenal mucosa converts trypsinogen to trypsin. Trypsin then activates all remaining zymogens. This cascade ensures proteolytic activity begins only in the duodenum, protecting the pancreas from autodigestion.

answers.text: The pancreatic duct is too narrow to transport large active enzyme molecules

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both zymogens and active enzymes are similar in molecular size. The duct can transport either form. The zymogen strategy is a safety mechanism against self-digestion, not a transport limitation.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key concept is autodigestion protection. Zymogens stay inactive until enterokinase activates trypsinogen → trypsin in the duodenum, which then activates all other zymogens — keeping the pancreas safe.
Exactly right. The zymogen cascade is a critical safety mechanism — when it fails (as in acute pancreatitis), premature enzyme activation causes the pancreas to digest itself.

params.question: Which of the following correctly describes the sequence of fat absorption in the small intestine?

answers.text: Bile salts chemically digest fat → fatty acids enter blood capillaries → travel via the portal vein to the liver

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bile salts emulsify fat (increase surface area) but do not chemically digest it — that is the role of pancreatic lipase. Also, absorbed fat enters lacteals (lymphatic vessels), not blood capillaries.

answers.text: Pancreatic lipase emulsifies fat droplets → products form micelles → chylomicrons enter blood capillaries

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Emulsification is performed by bile salts, not lipase. Lipase chemically digests fat after bile has emulsified it. Furthermore, chylomicrons enter lacteals (lymphatic vessels), not blood capillaries.

answers.text: Bile salts emulsify fat → pancreatic lipase releases fatty acids and monoglycerides → micelles carry them to the brush border → chylomicrons enter lacteals

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Bile salts first break fat into small droplets (emulsification), increasing the surface area for pancreatic lipase. The released fatty acids and monoglycerides are carried in micelles to the brush border. Inside the enterocyte, they are rebuilt into triglycerides, packaged into chylomicrons, and released into lacteals — bypassing portal circulation entirely.

answers.text: Pancreatic lipase acts on fat → bile salts package the products into micelles → chylomicrons are absorbed directly into portal blood

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The order is reversed — bile salts must emulsify fat before lipase can act effectively. Also, chylomicrons enter lacteals (lymphatic vessels), not portal blood. Dietary fat bypasses the liver on first pass.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the fat absorption pathway: bile salts emulsify → lipase digests → micelles transport → enterocyte rebuilds → chylomicrons → lacteals (lymphatic). The key point is that dietary fat bypasses portal circulation.

Well done. Understanding this sequence — emulsification, digestion, micelle transport, chylomicron formation, and lymphatic entry — explains why fat absorption is the most complex of all nutrient pathways.

params.question: Approximately 95% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver via portal blood. What is the clinical significance of this enterohepatic circulation?

answers.text: It ensures that bile salts are continuously available for vitamin B12 absorption in the ileum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Although the terminal ileum also absorbs the vitamin B12–intrinsic factor complex, this is a separate process. Bile salt recycling serves fat emulsification, not B12 absorption.

answers.text: Drugs that interrupt this cycle force the liver to synthesise new bile salts from cholesterol, thereby lowering LDL cholesterol

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Bile acid sequestrants bind bile salts in the gut and prevent reabsorption. The liver must then use cholesterol to synthesise replacement bile salts, depleting hepatic cholesterol stores and upregulating LDL receptors — ultimately lowering circulating LDL cholesterol.

answers.text: It prevents small intestinal bacterial overgrowth by maintaining high bile salt concentrations in the lumen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While bile salts do have some antimicrobial properties, prevention of bacterial overgrowth is primarily the role of the migrating myoelectric complex (MMC), driven by motilin during fasting.

answers.text: It allows the gallbladder to concentrate bile up to fifty times between meals

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The gallbladder concentrates bile up to ten times (not fifty) between meals by absorbing water and electrolytes. This concentration occurs independently of the enterohepatic recycling process.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key point is that the liver uses cholesterol to make bile salts. When drugs block bile salt reabsorption, the liver draws on its cholesterol stores to make more — this is how bile acid sequestrants lower LDL cholesterol.
Correct. The enterohepatic circulation recycles the bile salt pool 6–10 times daily. Interrupting this cycle with sequestrants is a well-established strategy for reducing LDL cholesterol.

params.question: A patient with cholera presents with profuse watery diarrhoea that continues despite complete fasting. Which type of diarrhoea does this pattern indicate?

answers.text: Osmotic diarrhoea

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Osmotic diarrhoea is caused by unabsorbed solutes drawing water into the gut lumen (e.g., in lactose intolerance). Its hallmark is that it stops when the patient fasts, since the unabsorbed solute is no longer being ingested.

answers.text: Secretory diarrhoea

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In secretory diarrhoea, active secretion of water and electrolytes into the gut lumen is driven by toxin-mediated mechanisms. Because this secretion is independent of dietary intake, it persists even during fasting — the hallmark that distinguishes it from osmotic diarrhoea.

answers.text: Inflammatory diarrhoea

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Inflammatory diarrhoea presents with blood or pus in the stool, as seen in ulcerative colitis or bacillary dysentery. Cholera produces profuse watery stool without blood or mucus.

answers.text: Malabsorptive diarrhoea

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Malabsorptive diarrhoea causes steatorrhoea — bulky, foul-smelling, fatty stools resulting from poor fat absorption (e.g., in coeliac disease or pancreatic insufficiency). Cholera does not impair absorption; it drives active secretion.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the fasting test: secretory diarrhoea (e.g., cholera) continues despite fasting because active ion secretion drives water loss. Osmotic diarrhoea stops when fasting removes the unabsorbed solute.
Exactly. The fasting test is a key clinical tool: secretory diarrhoea persists during fasting (toxin-driven secretion), while osmotic diarrhoea stops (no unabsorbed solute to draw water).
